title: Emission Arbitrator: KV-prefetch and Stall Mitigation for Streaming Outputs
content:
Purpose and summary:

This note proposes an "emission arbitrator" component that coordinates three concerns during token-streaming generation: (1) proactive KV-cache prefetching to avoid generation stalls, (2) an emit-credit-based arbitration for partial-token/chunk flushes to balance latency vs throughput, and (3) a coherent cancellation/rollback model that works with prefetch and partial emission. The goal is to reduce end-to-end user-visible stalls on long-context and cross-shard requests while keeping per-token costs and complexity bounded.

Motivation / observed problems:
- Users see occasional multi-100ms stalls mid-stream when the runtime must fetch KV shards from remote disks or rehydrate caches, causing token emission gaps.
- Current chunking policy uses fixed byte/bytepair thresholds which either flush too frequently (higher overhead) or infrequently (higher latency).
- Cancellation semantics are fuzzy when partial tokens (sub-token bytes or IVF-style micro-chunks) have been emitted and background prefetches are in-flight.

Design overview (high-level):
- Emission Arbitrator is a thin runtime layer sitting between the model kernel and transport layer. It receives candidate tokens from the kernel in micro-chunks (can be partial token pieces), tracks available "emit credits" per request, and decides when to flush to the client. It also subscribes to KV cache state events and drives prefetch requests when the upcoming attention windows indicate a high risk of eviction-caused stalls.
- The arbitrator exposes a small set of knobs in request config: min_emit_latency_ms, max_stall_budget_ms, kv_prefetch_aggressiveness (low/med/high), and emit_chunk_target_tokens.
- Scheduler integration: the arbitrator reports a per-request future-KV-access score to the scheduler; the scheduler may prioritize placement on nodes with warm KV or pre-apply faster path kernels to mitigate stall risk.

Key concepts and primitives:
1) Emit credits:
- Each request starts with a small number of emit credits proportional to immediate low-latency budget and client bandwidth estimate. Kernel micro-chunks consume credits; when credits deplete, arbitrator may hold subsequent micro-chunks until credits refill. Credits refill at a configured rate (tokens/sec smoothing) or when a kernel yields a completion boundary.
- Credits allow bursty emission early (good for perceived latency) and graceful smoothing later to maintain throughput without overwhelming network or provoking backpressure.

2) Prefetch planning window:
- Arbitrator maintains a rolling lookahead of N steps (default 32 tokens) using either (a) cached beam hypotheses or (b) a cheap next-token predictor heuristic to estimate KV keys that will be accessed.
- If predicted KV-key set contains items not in local KV LRU, arbitrator enqueues asynchronous prefetches with a priority derived from kv_prefetch_aggressiveness and expected time-to-use.

3) Stall budget and fast-fallback:
- Each request tracks a max_stall_budget_ms. If a prefetch miss would cause a stall that exceeds the budget, arbitrator triggers a fast-fallback policy: either (A) switch to smaller kernel variant with smaller memory working set (e.g., lower context kernel) or (B) emit a graceful placeholder (e.g., "..." partial token) and continue prefetch in background, with automatic patching if fallback output is later replaced. Decision depends on client support for patching streams.

4) Cancellation and rollback semantics:
- Cancellation can be requested by client or internal preemption. Arbitrator defines three cancellation phases: pre-emit, soft-emit, and confirmed-emit.
  - pre-emit: nothing sent, simple drop, cancel prefetch.
  - soft-emit: micro-chunks have been queued for transmission but not acknowledged by the network stack; cancel requests attempt to drain in-flight prefetches and issue a compensating abort.
  - confirmed-emit: bytes were acknowledged by client; we don't attempt removal but we attach provenance metadata (model-version, kernel-id, kv-snapshot) so downstream consumers can decide whether to accept as final or request re-evaluation.
- For cloud-hosted flows the arbitrator will include a 'patch_id' header for any fast-fallback emission so that later corrected tokens can be sent as patch messages and clients that support patches can reconcile.

Pseudocode (simplified):

function handle_kernel_chunk(req, chunk):
  if chunk.is_partial:
    if req.emit_credits > 0 or req.elapsed_since_last_emit > req.min_emit_latency_ms:
      flush(chunk)
      req.emit_credits -= chunk.credit_cost
      maybe_report_metric("emit.partial")
    else:
      queue_for_coalescing(req, chunk)
  else:  # full token
    flush(chunk)
    req.emit_credits = min(req.emit_credits + credit_recover, max_credits)
  // prefetch planning
  lookahead_keys = predict_keys(req, lookahead=32)
  for k in lookahead_keys:
    if not local_kv.contains(k) and not prefetch_queued(k):
      enqueue_prefetch(k, priority=pref_priority(req, k))
function on_prefetch_miss(req, key, estimated_latency_ms):
  if estimated_latency_ms > req.max_stall_budget_ms:
    trigger_fast_fallback(req)
  else:
    allow_prefetch_and_hold_emission(req)

Configuration knobs (proposal):
- emit_chunk_target_tokens: integer (default 4) -- soft target for coalescing micro-chunks into larger emits when credits allow.
- min_emit_latency_ms: integer (default 25) -- minimum perceived latency between first discovery and first byte emit.
- max_stall_budget_ms: integer (default 150) -- maximum tolerable stall before fallback.
- kv_prefetch_aggressiveness: enum {low, medium, high} -- controls how many KV keys to prefetch and priority threshold.
- emit_patch_strategy: enum {none, patch-on-correction, always-send} -- how corrected fallback outputs are reconciled.

Metrics to capture and alert on:
- stream_stall_events_per_1k: count of stalls where pause > 50ms between pulses.
- prefetch_miss_latency: histogram of latency when a requested KV shard is not local.
- emit_patch_rate: percent of streams that required patch corrections after fast-fallback.
- average_emit_credit_utilization: how often credits are depleted and cause coalescing.

Operational considerations and rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (lab): implement arbitrator stub on a single experimental pool; collect metrics and assert no client-observable diffs for standard short prompts. Feature flags: kv_prefetch disabled by default.
- Phase 2 (canary): enable kv_prefetch=medium for 5% of traffic; enable emit_patch_strategy=patch-on-correction for clients with patch support. Monitor stream_stall_events and emit_patch_rate.
- Phase 3 (wider): tune default knobs based on latency and cost tradeoffs; consider scheduler hints to prefer warm-kv nodes for long-context requests.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Prediction accuracy vs prefetch cost: aggressive prefetch reduces stalls but increases egress and cache churn. We need a live A/B to tune kv_prefetch_aggressiveness by workload class.
- Kernel variant switching cost: how expensive is swapping kernel versions mid-request compared to waiting for a prefetch?
- Client compatibility for patch-on-correction: many early SDKs don't support patches; default should be conservative.
- How to credit back prefetch cost to customer billing when prefetch was speculative? (billing/product question)

Immediate TODOs:
- Spike: implement a lightweight next-token predictor based on recent token distribution; evaluate precision/recall for prefetch keys. Owner: Marcus. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Instrumentation: add stream_stall_events_per_1k, prefetch_miss_latency histogram. Owner: Rosa. ETA: 1 week.
- Prototype: implement emission arbitrator state machine with emit credits on dev pool. Owner: Aisha. ETA: 3 weeks.

Appendix: sample emitted metadata header (for each flushed chunk)
- model-version: vX.YZ
- kernel-id: kernel-2025-02-optim
- kv-snapshot-id: kvs-20250214-a1b2
- patch_id: uuid (only if fallback/patch used)

This design prioritizes reducing user-visible mid-stream stalls while keeping emitted outputs reconcilable. It is intentionally conservative about irreversible client-visible changes (confirmed-emit) and biases toward patchable fast-fallbacks in environments where the client SDK supports correction. Feedback wanted on: preferred defaults for max_stall_budget_ms and whether the scheduler should expose an API for arbitrator stall-scores.
